verdicts.text: Pulumi packages come in two flavors (source-based and executable-based), and each is versioned and released differently.
verdicts.evidence: The sibling guide packaging-components.md names the same two Pulumi-package kinds: a "Source-based plugin package — a Pulumi package distributed as source" and an "Executable-based plugin package — a Pulumi package whose plugin is a pre-built executable". It also describes different distribution for each: a Git ref/tag vs. a pre-built binary plus SDKs. Native language packages are the third option there, but that page calls them "Not a Pulumi package", so saying there are two flavors holds.
verdicts.framing_note: This is a taxonomy statement, and it matches the sibling docs page. That page is from the same site, so it backs the claim up but isn't independent product source. That's why confidence is medium.

verdicts.text: The Pulumi IDP Private Registry documentation is located at /docs/idp/concepts/private-registry/; packaging-components page has anchors #source-based-plugin-packages and #executable-based-plugin-packages; CLI reference exists at /docs/iac/cli/commands/pulumi_package_publish/.
verdicts.evidence: All three targets are in the repo. content/docs/idp/concepts/private-registry.md exists with the title "Private Registry". packaging-components.md contains the headings "## Source-based plugin packages" and "## Executable-based plugin packages", which produce the #source-based-plugin-packages and #executable-based-plugin-packages anchors. The auto-generated content/docs/iac/cli/commands/pulumi_package_publish.md exists and reads "Publish a package to the Private Registry".

verdicts.text: Publishing a source-based package to the Private Registry requires applying a semver Git tag (e.g., v1.2.3) to the repository.
verdicts.evidence: The Private Registry docs agree: "Pulumi uses git tags for versioning components... The tag must adhere to the semantic versioning standard plus a "v" prefix (e.g. `v1.2.3`)". Its troubleshooting table also lists "`error: no version tag found` | Tag your repository with a semver tag". I couldn't confirm this against the CLI source because GitHub code search was rate-limited.
verdicts.framing_note: This is support from another Pulumi docs page, not from product source.

verdicts.text: `pulumi package publish` sends the package metadata to Pulumi Cloud and places the package in the Private Registry.
verdicts.evidence: The auto-generated CLI reference, built from pulumi/pulumi cobra source, says: "This command publishes a package to the Private Registry. The package can be a provider or a schema." It also describes pulling out the package schema and README, which is the metadata the claim says gets sent to Pulumi Cloud.
verdicts.framing_note: The source says 'Publish a package to the Private Registry'. The claim says it 'sends the package metadata to Pulumi Cloud and places the package in the Private Registry', which puts the same thing in different words.

verdicts.text: Semver-tagged releases are only required for publishing to the Pulumi Private Registry.
verdicts.evidence: The auto-generated CLI reference (transcribed from pulumi/pulumi source) says a Git-referenced package version "can either be a tag (in semver format), or a Git commit hash." That means semver still applies outside the Private Registry for tags, and nothing says branches or non-semver tags work. So the claim that semver tags are required "only" for the Private Registry, and the next sentence saying "any Git ref (tag, branch, or commit)" works, overstate what's supported. Commit hashes do skip semver.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Check pulumi/pulumi's plugin git-ref resolution (pkg/workspace) to confirm whether branch names or non-semver tags work in Pulumi.yaml package refs; the gh code search was rate-limited.

verdicts.text: Source-based packages referenced directly from a `Pulumi.yaml` file can use any Git ref (tag, branch, or commit), regardless of whether it is a valid semantic version.
verdicts.evidence: I couldn't check this claim. Sibling docs only show consumers adding a package at a tag (for example, "consumers can then run `pulumi package add <repo-url>@<tag>`" in source-based-plugin.md). None of them say that branches, commits, or non-semver refs are supported. I tried to confirm in pulumi/pulumi source how non-semver `@ref` values in Pulumi.yaml package specs get resolved, but the GitHub API hit its rate limit (HTTP 429/403) first.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Any Git ref (tag, branch, or commit)" is a broad claim. As far as I remember (not checked this session), Pulumi's plugin spec handles commit hashes as pseudo-versions, but I'm not sure it supports branch names. Someone should check pulumi/pulumi sdk/go/common/workspace plugin spec parsing.

verdicts.text: Executable-based package releases are produced by a CI/CD pipeline that builds the plugin, generates the SDKs, and pushes everything to the relevant feeds.
verdicts.evidence: The tag-triggered release workflow in Pulumi's own provider boilerplate matches the described pipeline. It runs `make provider` ("Build Provider"), then a build_sdks matrix job for nodejs/python/dotnet/go/java ("Generate SDK: make generate_${{ matrix.language }}"), then publishes the artifacts.
verdicts.framing_note: The sentence has no hedge, but it describes the usual practice. Releases could also be built by hand, so this is a recommended pattern rather than a strict requirement.

verdicts.evidence: The link target exists: packaging-components.md has the heading "## Executable-based plugin packages" (L73), so the #executable-based-plugin-packages anchor resolves. That section backs the description: "Executable-based plugin packages are usually distributed as pre-built per-language SDKs published to multiple package managers (one per consumer language), with the plugin executable published to an accessible location."
verdicts.framing_note: Claim says 'pre-built plugin binary, typically alongside per-language SDKs published to package feeds'; source says 'usually distributed as pre-built per-language SDKs ... with the plugin executable published to an accessible location'. The two say the same thing.

verdicts.text: In both source-based and executable-based cases, the released artifact is a single, semantically-versioned Pulumi package.
verdicts.evidence: This line summarizes the two sections above it: source-based releases use "a semver Git tag (for example, `v1.2.3`)", and for executable-based packages "the package's version is the version embedded in the published binary and SDKs." The sibling packaging-components page describes both flavors as a single "Pulumi package" released at one version. One caveat: L24 of the same page says semver is "only required for publishing to the Private Registry", and direct Git-ref consumption can use any ref. So "semantically-versioned" holds only for formal releases.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The broad "semantically-versioned" wording is qualified by the page's own L24 (any Git ref works when a source-based package is consumed directly). I found no independent product-source check.

verdicts.text: A repository containing multiple Pulumi packages either has to release them in lockstep or invent per-package release tooling that fights the way Pulumi naturally consumes packages.
verdicts.evidence: I couldn't check this against an independent source. The sentence is mostly Pulumi's own editorial recommendation ("A repository should contain exactly one Pulumi package"). The testable part is that per-package release tooling "fights the way Pulumi naturally consumes packages". My gh searches of pulumi/pulumi code and issues for tag handling when a package lives in a repo subdirectory returned nothing, so I couldn't confirm or rule out that Pulumi handles per-package tags (e.g., a subdirectory prefix) natively.
verdicts.source: repo:content/docs/iac/guides/building-extending/packages/repository-strategy.md L34; gh search code/issues -R pulumi/pulumi (no results)
verdicts.intuition_flag: If Pulumi resolves git refs for packages in subdirectories (e.g., `pulumi package add github.com/org/repo/subdir@vX`), the "fights the way Pulumi naturally consumes packages" wording may overstate things. Worth confirming with the packages team.

verdicts.text: A 1:1 repository-to-package mapping keeps git tags, release artifacts, and version history aligned.
verdicts.evidence: In context (L32-34), this sentence is the rationale for Pulumi's own editorial recommendation ("A repository should contain exactly one Pulumi package"). It's a best-practice argument that follows from the page's premise that the package is the unit of versioning. It doesn't describe a specific product behavior that source code could confirm or refute.

verdicts.text: Multiple components inside a single Pulumi package are fine and expected, and the components ship together at the package's version.
verdicts.evidence: The package schema reference has a single package-level version ("`version` | `string` | Yes | Version is the version of the package. The version must be valid semver.") and a `resources` map that can hold many resources, including components (`isComponent: true`). So every component in a package ships at that one package version. The "fine and expected" part is Pulumi's own recommendation, not a checkable fact.
verdicts.framing_note: The schema doc mirrors the product metaschema. I couldn't confirm directly against the pulumi/pulumi source because gh search was rate-limited (HTTP 429).

verdicts.text: One `PulumiPlugin.yaml` at the repository root defines the package, with components living alongside it in the repository.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass3) The source-based plugin guide agrees: every example layout has `PulumiPlugin.yaml` at the plugin root, and it says "A single plugin package can expose **multiple components**" and "Pulumi reads `PulumiPlugin.yaml`, introspects the plugin". One caveat: the manifest only declares the runtime. The package/SDK name comes from the language manifest (package.json, pyproject.toml and so on), so "defines the package" is a loose way to put it.
verdicts.framing_note: Checked only against a sibling docs page, not against Pulumi's own source code. The example tree nests components under a components/ subdirectory; that works only if the entry file exports or registers them (in Go, components must be listed explicitly). The example leaves out the language manifest and the entry file.

verdicts.text: The example repository layout places a single `PulumiPlugin.yaml` at the repo root with components under a `components/` directory (EksCluster/, EksIam/) as a valid layout for a Pulumi package.
verdicts.evidence: The sibling packaging guide describes a source-based plugin package as needing "`PulumiPlugin.yaml` plus an entry file" and puts no restrictions on subdirectories, so a root `PulumiPlugin.yaml` with component code under `components/` is a valid layout. The entry file (e.g. index.ts or __main__.py, which must export or import the components) is left out of the example as `...`, which is reasonable for an illustration.
verdicts.framing_note: I couldn't check component discovery from subdirectories in product source because the GitHub code search was rate-limited (HTTP 429).

verdicts.text: When unrelated components share a package, every release of the package versions every component the same way, regardless of whether each component changed, which violates semver.
verdicts.evidence: This is Pulumi's own advice explaining why it recommends one cohesive package per repository, not a checkable product behavior. The factual core, that components share their package's single version, matches how packages work: a package schema carries one `version`, and the guide says components "inherit the package's version." Whether that "violates semver" is the author's opinion, not a fact.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Strictly speaking, SemVer 2.0 versions a package's public API as a whole, so bumping the version when some component didn't change doesn't break the spec. It only makes the version less useful as a signal for each component. The author might soften "violates semver" to "undermines semver's signal."

verdicts.text: In the example, an enhancement to ComponentA releases the package at v1.1.0 (minor bump from v1.0.0), and a breaking change to ComponentB releases the package at v2.0.0 (major bump), per semver.
verdicts.evidence: The SemVer spec says to bump "MINOR version when you add functionality in a backward compatible manner", and that major "MUST be incremented if any backward incompatible changes are introduced to the public API" (resetting minor and patch to 0). So v1.0.0 → v1.1.0 for an enhancement, then → v2.0.0 for a breaking change, follows the spec.
verdicts.framing_note: The doc's ComponentA/ComponentB version numbers are the author's own illustration. The specific bumps in it are special cases of the general SemVer MAJOR/MINOR rules.
